title: Female External Genitalia and Sexuality Terms
body:
## What it is
The vulva is the collective name for the female external genitalia. Before the anatomy, three terms are kept apart: **sexuality** is the whole mix of feelings, attitudes, preferences and behaviors tied to being sexual; **gender** is the inner sense of being feminine or masculine; **sex** is biologic male or female status.

## Must-know structures
- **Mons pubis (mons veneris):** fat pad over the symphysis pubis, hair-covered after puberty.
- **Labia majora:** two large fatty folds that protect the urethral and vaginal openings.
- **Labia minora:** two hairless folds inside the majora.
- **Clitoris:** small erectile organ with many nerve endings; the site of sexual arousal.
- **Fourchette:** where the labia join at the back; a common site of episiotomy cuts and tears.
- **Vestibule:** almond-shaped area holding the urinary meatus, Skene's glands, the hymen, the vaginal opening and Bartholin's glands.
- **Skene's (paraurethral) glands:** a little mucus for lubrication.
- **Bartholin's (paravaginal) glands:** alkaline secretion that neutralizes vaginal acidity, helping sperm survive.
- **Hymen:** thin membrane partly covering the vaginal opening.
- **Perineum:** the muscular area between the vagina and anus.

## How the exam asks about it
Identify a structure from its function (episiotomy site = fourchette/perineum; alkaline secretion = Bartholin's). Questions on episiotomy care and perineal tears come back in [[Fourth Stage of Labor and Postpartum Checks]] and [[Postpartum Infection and Endometritis]].

## Related topics
[[Female Internal Genitalia: Vagina, Uterus and Decidua]], [[Male Reproductive Anatomy]]

title: Female Internal Genitalia: Vagina, Uterus and Decidua
body:
## Vagina
A stretchy canal that serves as the passage for menstrual flow and the baby. The anterior wall is about 6-7 cm and the posterior wall 8-9 cm. Rugae (thick folds) let it stretch without tearing during birth.

## Uterus
A hollow, pear-shaped muscular organ that houses and feeds the fetus. Non-pregnant it is about 5-7 cm long, 5 cm wide, 2.5 cm thick and weighs about 60 g; in pregnancy it becomes ovoid and weighs about 1000 g.

Parts:
- **Fundus:** top part, palpated through the abdomen to follow uterine growth.
- **Corpus (body):** expands to hold the growing fetus.
- **Isthmus:** short segment between body and cervix; the part usually cut in a cesarean birth.
- **Cervix:** lowest part, about half above and half inside the vagina.

Layers, inside to outside:
- **Endometrium:** inner lining (basal and glandular layers); what is shed in menstruation.
- **Myometrium:** muscle layer; it contracts in labor and also closes off the tubal junctions to stop menstrual blood backing up into the tubes.
- **Perimetrium:** outer layer giving strength and support.

## Decidua
"Decidua" means falling off. In pregnancy the endometrium becomes the decidua:
- **Basalis:** under the embryo (becomes the maternal side of the placenta).
- **Capsularis:** stretches over the embryo surface.
- **Vera:** the rest of the lining.

## How the exam asks about it
Fundal height as the way to track growth ([[Fundic Height Landmarks in Pregnancy]]), and the isthmus as the cesarean incision site.

## Related topics
[[Female External Genitalia and Sexuality Terms]], [[Ovaries and Fallopian Tubes]], [[Phases of the Menstrual Cycle]]

title: Ovaries and Fallopian Tubes
body:
## Ovaries
Almond-shaped, grayish-white female gonads (about 4 cm long). They **produce, mature and release ova** and make **estrogen and progesterone**, which start and regulate the menstrual cycle ([[Hormonal Control of the Menstrual Cycle]]).

## Fallopian tubes
About 10 cm long. They carry the ovum to the uterus and are where sperm meet the ovum (fertilization). Segments, from ovary to uterus:
- **Infundibulum:** funnel-shaped, about 2 cm, with finger-like fimbriae that sweep the ovum in.
- **Ampulla:** the longest segment; the usual site of fertilization **and the most common site of ectopic pregnancy**.
- **Isthmus:** the narrow part cut or sealed in tubal ligation (permanent sterilization).
- **Interstitial portion:** inside the uterine wall; the **most dangerous** ectopic site because rupture is worst here.

## Why it matters
Tube anatomy explains why an implanted embryo in the tube can rupture and bleed into the abdomen ([[Ectopic Pregnancy]]). Ligation at the isthmus ties into family planning ([[Reproductive Health and Family Planning]]).

## Related topics
[[Female Internal Genitalia: Vagina, Uterus and Decidua]], [[Ectopic Pregnancy]]

title: Male Reproductive Anatomy
body:
## External structures
- **Penis:** organ for urination and intercourse. Two corpora cavernosa (side columns of erectile tissue) and one corpus spongiosum on the underside.
- **Scrotum:** pouch holding the testes; it acts as a temperature regulator for them.
- **Testes:** two ovoid glands, 2-3 cm wide, sitting in the scrotum.

## Internal structures in the order sperm travel
- **Epididymis:** collects sperm from the testis and is where they mature.
- **Vas deferens:** carries sperm up through the inguinal canal into the abdomen.
- **Seminal vesicle:** adds the thick part of the semen (fructose, protein, prostaglandin).
- **Ejaculatory duct:** joins the seminal vesicle to the urethra.
- **Prostate gland:** alkaline fluid that protects sperm and reduces vaginal acidity.
- **Cowper's (bulbourethral) gland:** lubricating fluid into the urethra.
- **Urethra:** shared passage for urine and semen.

## How the exam asks about it
Match structure to function (fructose = seminal vesicle; sperm maturation = epididymis). Useful for family planning teaching such as vasectomy ([[Reproductive Health and Family Planning]]).

## Related topics
[[Female External Genitalia and Sexuality Terms]], [[Hormonal Control of the Menstrual Cycle]]

title: Hormonal Control of the Menstrual Cycle
body:
## Normal values from the handout
- Average cycle 28 days (range 23-35).
- Flow lasts about 4-6 days normally (1-9 counts as abnormal in the handout).
- Normal blood loss about 30-80 mL (roughly a quarter cup).

## The four-organ chain
1. **Hypothalamus** releases GnRH.
2. **Anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis)** is stimulated to release the gonadotropins.
3. **Ovaries** respond by maturing a follicle, ovulating, and making estrogen and progesterone.
4. **Uterus** builds its lining (stratum functionalis) for a possible pregnancy and sheds it if none happens.

## The two gonadotropins
- **FSH:** active early in the cycle; matures the primordial follicle.
- **LH:** most active at mid-cycle; the LH surge triggers ovulation.

## How the exam asks about it
Which hormone triggers ovulation (LH surge), which organ is the "master" (hypothalamus), and what the lining does when no pregnancy happens. The phases are detailed in [[Phases of the Menstrual Cycle]].

## Memory aid
"FSH = follicle first; LH = let go (ovulate)". Made up, not from the handout.

## Related topics
[[Phases of the Menstrual Cycle]], [[Ovaries and Fallopian Tubes]]

title: Phases of the Menstrual Cycle
body:
## Proliferative (follicular/estrogenic/post-menstrual) phase
- First phase, **length varies** (about 6-14 days in the handout).
- Just after flow the lining is very thin. Rising **estrogen** makes it grow, thickening it many-fold (about 1 mm to 8 mm).
- One follicle matures per cycle: the **Graafian follicle**, the most mature, full of estrogen-rich fluid with an ovum ready to leave.
- Peak estrogen triggers the **LH surge**, and the ovum is released: **ovulation**.

## Luteal (secretory/progestational/premenstrual) phase
- Second phase, **always about 14 days** (constant).
- The empty follicle becomes the **corpus luteum**, which makes **progesterone**.
- Progesterone maintains and organizes the lining; the glands become twisted (corkscrew) and secretory. Note: the handout also says LH peaks here, which conflicts with LH peaking at ovulation; see the check section.

## Ischemic phase
If there is no fertilization, the corpus luteum regresses after about 8-10 days. Estrogen and progesterone fall, capillaries rupture, and the lining begins to slough.

## Menstrual phase
Estrogen and progesterone are lowest; menstrual flow passes.

## Clinical tie-in
Depo-Provera (a progesterone preparation) is used for dysfunctional uterine bleeding.

## How the exam asks about it
Which phase is variable (proliferative) versus constant (luteal), and what hormone dominates each. A pregnancy test or a missed period is the reference point used in [[Signs of Pregnancy: Presumptive, Probable and Positive]].

## Check against your textbook
- The handout says LH "peaks" in the luteal phase; textbooks place the LH surge just before ovulation, with the corpus luteum then making progesterone.
- Confirm the exact day ranges for the phases; they vary by source.

## Related topics
[[Hormonal Control of the Menstrual Cycle]], [[Female Internal Genitalia: Vagina, Uterus and Decidua]]

title: Obstetric Terms: Zygote to Viability and Gravida-TPAL
body:
## Stages of prenatal development (age of gestation, AOG)
- **Zygote:** result of fertilization, up to about 2 weeks.
- **Embryo:** from implantation until organs form, about 2 to under 8 weeks.
- **Fetus:** 8 weeks to birth.
- **Implantation:** the growing structure attaches to the endometrium about 8-10 days after fertilization.

## Viability
The fetus can live outside the uterus: **24 weeks and above** per the handout (elsewhere it also mentions 500 g, see [[Spontaneous and Induced Abortion]]).

## Gravida and TPAL
- **Gravida:** number of pregnancies, counted regardless of outcome.
- **TPAL:** **T**erm births (38-42 weeks in the handout), **P**reterm births (under 37 weeks), **A**bortions, **L**iving children.
- **Nulligravid:** never pregnant.
- **Nullipara:** has never delivered a viable infant. The handout's wording mixes this up with gravidity.

## Worked example (made up)
A woman who is pregnant for the third time, with one earlier term baby and one earlier preterm baby (both alive), is G3 and T1 P1 A0 L2: the current pregnancy counts toward gravida but not yet toward para.

## How the exam asks about it
Computing G and TPAL from a short history, and telling embryo from fetus by weeks.

## Check against your textbook
- "Nulliparous" in the handout ("had been pregnant before but never given birth to a viable infant") is a muddled definition; check your local textbook.
- Term is usually 37-42 weeks; the handout says 38-42.

## Related topics
[[Signs of Pregnancy: Presumptive, Probable and Positive]], [[Post-term Pregnancy]]

title: Signs of Pregnancy: Presumptive, Probable and Positive
body:
## How the three groups differ
- **Presumptive:** subjective, felt by the woman; least reliable.
- **Probable:** can be documented by the examiner; still not proof.
- **Positive:** only the fetus itself can cause it; diagnostic.

## Presumptive signs
- Breast tenderness, fullness, darker areola.
- Nausea and vomiting (rising hCG). Relief: dry unsalted crackers, ice chips, small frequent low-fat meals, ambulation.
- Amenorrhea.
- Urinary frequency (uterus presses on the bladder, first and third trimesters).
- Fatigue (higher metabolic need).
- **Quickening:** mother feels fetal movement at about 18-20 weeks.
- Skin changes: melasma/chloasma (mask of pregnancy), linea nigra (pubis to navel), striae gravidarum (silvery stretch marks).

## Probable signs
- Positive pregnancy test (hCG), detectable about 10-14 days after the missed period; hCG peaks about 10 weeks.
- Abdominal enlargement, symmetrical and globular ([[Fundic Height Landmarks in Pregnancy]]).
- **Chadwick's:** bluish-purple vagina/cervix from more blood vessels.
- **Goodell's:** softened cervix.
- **Hegar's:** softened lower uterine segment.
- **Ballottement:** fetus rebounds when the lower uterus is tapped, about 16-20 weeks.
- **Braxton-Hicks:** periodic painless tightening, from about 28 weeks.

## Positive signs
- Fetal heart tones.
- Fetal movement felt by the examiner.
- Fetus seen on ultrasound or X-ray ([[Ultrasound in Pregnancy]]).

## How the exam asks about it
Classify a finding into presumptive/probable/positive. Nausea and quickening are presumptive; Chadwick's and a positive hCG test are probable; fetal heart tones are positive.

## Memory aid
Positive signs = "the baby itself shows up". Made up.

## Related topics
[[Obstetric Terms: Zygote to Viability and Gravida-TPAL]], [[Fundic Height Landmarks in Pregnancy]], [[Prenatal Visits, Blood Pressure and Leopold's Maneuvers]]
outlineRefs: Pregnancy: Presumptive, Probable and Positive Signs

title: Fundic Height Landmarks in Pregnancy
body:
## What it is
Measuring from the top of the symphysis pubis to the top of the fundus with a tape (centimeters) is a quick way to estimate the age of gestation and spot growth problems.

## Landmarks from the handout
- **12 weeks:** fundus at the symphysis pubis.
- **16 weeks:** halfway between symphysis and umbilicus.
- **20 weeks:** at the umbilicus.
- Each additional centimeter above the umbilicus is about 4 more weeks: +1 cm = 24 weeks, +2 = 28, +3 = 32, +4 = 36 weeks (xiphoid level).
- **40 weeks:** about 1 cm below the xiphoid process (the baby drops/engages before labor).

## Nursing points
- The woman lies supine with legs flexed for abdominal assessment; use the centimeter side of the tape.
- A fundus much bigger than expected suggests multiple pregnancy ([[Multiple Pregnancy and Twin Types]]), hydramnios or a mole ([[Hydatidiform Mole]]); smaller than expected suggests poor fetal growth or oligohydramnios ([[Amniocentesis and Amniotic Fluid]]).

## How the exam asks about it
Estimate weeks of gestation from a fundal level, or decide what an unexpectedly large uterus might mean.

## Check against your textbook
The "+1 cm = 4 weeks" rule above the umbilicus is the handout's simplification; the common McDonald's rule is fundal height in cm approximately equals weeks of gestation after about 20 weeks.

## Related topics
[[Signs of Pregnancy: Presumptive, Probable and Positive]], [[Prenatal Visits, Blood Pressure and Leopold's Maneuvers]]

title: Prenatal Visits, Blood Pressure and Leopold's Maneuvers
body:
## Prenatal visit schedule
- Up to 28 weeks: every 4 weeks.
- 28-36 weeks: every 2 weeks.
- 36 weeks onward: every week.

## Taking blood pressure
Rest the mother about 15 minutes first. Position changes the reading: **sitting highest, supine in between, left lateral lowest**. Use the same position each visit for fair comparison.

## Abdominal assessment
Supine, legs flexed. Inspect for striae and linea nigra, then measure fundic height ([[Fundic Height Landmarks in Pregnancy]]).

## Leopold's maneuvers
Purpose: find fetal presentation and position.

Preparation, and why:
- Have her void first: a full bladder blocks palpation and is uncomfortable.
- Knees slightly flexed, small pillow or towel under one side: relaxes the abdomen and tilts the uterus off the vena cava, preventing supine hypotensive syndrome.
- Warm hands/water: comfort and no abdominal tightening.
- Face her head for maneuvers 1-3; face her feet for the fourth.

The four:
1. **Fundal:** what lies in the fundus; head (firm, round, moves separately) or breech (softer, moves with the body). Gives presentation.
2. **Lateral:** locates the fetal **back** (smooth, hard). Knobby parts are limbs. **Fetal heart tones are heard best over the back.**
3. **Pelvic (Pawlik):** what sits at the inlet and whether it is engaged. Not engaged = it moves up or sideways; engaged = firmly settled.
4. **Pelvic brim:** attitude and degree of extension; done only if the fetus is cephalic.

## How the exam asks about it
Where to place the stethoscope for fetal heart tones, why the mother voids first, and why a pillow is used under one side. Position terms are in [[Fetal Lie, Attitude, Presentation, Position and Station]].

## Related topics
[[Fundic Height Landmarks in Pregnancy]], [[Fetal Lie, Attitude, Presentation, Position and Station]], [[Body Changes in Pregnancy: Heart, Blood and Lungs]]

title: Body Changes in Pregnancy: Heart, Blood and Lungs
body:
## Cardiovascular
- Heart is pushed upward, left and forward.
- Cardiac output rises about 25-50%; heart rate rises about 10 bpm.
- Pressure from the uterus on veins slows circulation, causing edema and varicosities of legs, vulva and rectum.
- **Supine hypotensive syndrome:** the uterus presses on the vena cava when lying flat. **Position of choice: left lateral (Sims').**

## Blood
Plasma volume rises more than red cells, so blood is diluted: **physiologic anemia**. Teach iron-rich foods and supplements to meet higher iron needs.

## Respiratory
- Shortness of breath from uterine enlargement.
- Oxygen use up as much as 20% and breathing volume up to 40%.
- Tendency to over-breathe (hyperventilate), causing respiratory alkalosis: tingling in the extremities, light-headedness. Help: breathe slowly into a paper bag or cupped hands.

## Priority nursing action
For dizziness or a low BP when supine, turn her to her left side first (restores venous return; Maslow: circulation before teaching).

## How the exam asks about it
Why physiologic anemia is "normal" yet iron is still given, and the best position for a pregnant woman. Heart disease implications are in [[Heart Disease in Pregnancy]].

## Related topics
[[Body Changes in Pregnancy: Digestive, Kidney, Thyroid and Back]], [[Heart Disease in Pregnancy]]

title: Body Changes in Pregnancy: Digestive, Kidney, Thyroid and Back
body:
## Digestive discomforts
- **Pica:** craving non-food substances (clay, chalk, dirt, starch). Counsel on risks and check for anemia.
- **Epulis:** gum swelling that bleeds easily (estrogen). Use a soft toothbrush, avoid strong mouthwash.
- **Ptyalism:** excess saliva. Hard candies can help.
- **Heartburn:** the uterus crowds the stomach and slows emptying. Do not lie down after eating, walk gently, eat small frequent meals.

## Kidney and bladder
Hormones relax the ureters and renal pelvis and the growing uterus compresses the bladder: urinary **frequency** and urine stasis, so higher **UTI risk**.

## Thyroid
The handout warns that hyperthyroidism is a pregnancy risk and thyroid storm (arrhythmias, possible death) is dangerous in labor. Watch for its signs.

## Muscles and bones
- **Relaxin** loosens pelvic joints.
- **Diastasis recti:** rectus muscles separate; normal and recovers after birth.
- **Physiologic lordosis** ("pride of pregnancy") and back pain: pelvic rocking, direct pressure on the lumbar area, avoid lying flat; the handout says no analgesics.

## How the exam asks about it
Match a discomfort with the best self-care measure. Safe, non-drug measures first (assess, teach, then medicate).

## Check against your textbook
- The handout says pica may come from hypersalivation; the usual teaching links it to nutrient deficiency or cultural factors.
- "No analgesic" for back pain should be checked with your textbook and prescriber guidance.
- "Greatest risk for hyperthyroidism" is worded loosely.

## Related topics
[[Body Changes in Pregnancy: Heart, Blood and Lungs]], [[Postpartum Infection and Endometritis]]
outlineRefs: Gastrointestinal Tract: Pica, Epulis, Ptyalism, Heartburn

title: Drugs to Avoid in Pregnancy: NSAIDs and Aspirin
body:
## NSAIDs (example: indomethacin)
- Not advisable in pregnancy.
- Cause **premature closure of the ductus arteriosus**, so blood flow to the lower half of the fetal body is cut.
- Reduce fetal urine output, leading to **oligohydramnios**.
- Neonatal problems after prenatal exposure listed in the handout: pulmonary hypertension, necrotizing enterocolitis, intracranial hemorrhage, cystic brain lesions, kidney dysfunction.

## Aspirin
Possible effects: bleeding, early ductus closure, pulmonary hypertension, prolonged pregnancy and labor, growth restriction, and salicylate toxicity in the baby. Teaching from the handout: **low-dose only, and stop about four weeks before the due date.**

## Priority nursing actions
Ask about all drugs, herbs and over-the-counter products at each prenatal visit; advise the pregnant woman not to self-medicate and to check with her midwife or doctor first (safety of the fetus).

## How the exam asks about it
Which common pain reliever to avoid and the fetal effect (ductus arteriosus closure). Related to post-term risk in [[Post-term Pregnancy]].

## Check against your textbook
Doses and whether low-dose aspirin is advised depend on the indication; do not rely on this note for prescribing.

## Related topics
[[Body Changes in Pregnancy: Digestive, Kidney, Thyroid and Back]], [[Post-term Pregnancy]]
outlineRefs: Frequent used drugs that should not be taken during pregnancy

title: Amniocentesis and Amniotic Fluid
body:
## What it is
Withdrawing amniotic fluid through the abdominal wall for testing. Best at about **14-16 weeks** (second trimester) in the handout.

## Amniotic fluid facts
- Normal volume about 800-1200 mL.
- **Oligohydramnios:** under 500 mL. **Polyhydramnios (hydramnios):** over 1200 mL.
- Normal color clear to slightly yellow. **Strong yellow** suggests blood incompatibility; **green** means meconium.

## Nursing actions
Before: the woman **voids** (a smaller bladder avoids accidental puncture). After: observe about **30 minutes**, checking fetal heart rate and for uterine contractions (risk of labor or fetal distress).

## What the fluid can show
- **Fetal lung maturity:** lecithin-sphingomyelin ratio, normal 2:1 (lecithin = lung surfactant). Useful if early delivery is considered.
- **Bilirubin** when blood incompatibility is suspected; the sample must not contain blood or the result is falsely positive.
- Inborn errors of metabolism, e.g. cystinosis and maple syrup urine disease.

## How the exam asks about it
Pre- and post-procedure care, and what L:S ratio means. Compare with the less invasive tests in [[Ultrasound in Pregnancy]] and [[Chorionic Villi Sampling and Alpha-Fetoprotein]].

## Check against your textbook
Gestation timing varies by purpose (genetic testing is usually 15-20 weeks; lung maturity later). Confirm.

## Related topics
[[Ultrasound in Pregnancy]], [[Chorionic Villi Sampling and Alpha-Fetoprotein]], [[HELLP Syndrome]]

title: Ultrasound in Pregnancy
body:
## What it is
Sound waves bounce off tissues to make a picture. Non-invasive and used all through pregnancy.

## Preparing the client
- **Transabdominal:** drink plenty of water about an hour before; a full bladder pushes the uterus into view.
- **Transvaginal:** have her void first.

## First trimester findings
Confirms pregnancy (cardiac movement, yolk sac, fetal heart tone), shows whether an intrauterine device is in place, and identifies a hydatidiform mole: "snowstorm" pattern of white specks on a dark background ([[Hydatidiform Mole]]).

## Second and third trimester findings
Placenta location (for previa, [[Placenta Previa]]), fetal growth, amniotic fluid amount, fetal position and presentation, and sex (possible from about 16 weeks; clearer later). 3D ultrasound may show structural problems.

## Related use
Ultrasound makes up part of the biophysical profile ([[Biophysical Profile and Non-Stress Test]]).

## How the exam asks about it
Client preparation (full vs empty bladder) and what a snowstorm appearance indicates.

## Related topics
[[Amniocentesis and Amniotic Fluid]], [[Placenta Previa]], [[Hydatidiform Mole]]

title: Biophysical Profile and Non-Stress Test
body:
## Biophysical profile (BPP)
Five components: fetal reactivity (non-stress test), breathing movement, tone, amniotic fluid volume, and fetal movement/activity. It can be done as often as daily in high-risk pregnancies.

Score 2 criteria from the handout (ultrasound parts):
- **Breathing:** one episode of at least 30 seconds within 30 minutes.
- **Movement:** at least three limb or trunk movements in 30 minutes.
- **Tone:** at least one extension then flexion in 30 minutes.
- **Fluid:** a pocket over 1 cm vertically.
- **NST:** two or more accelerations of at least 15 bpm lasting 15 seconds in 20 minutes.

Interpretation (handout): **8-10 = doing well; 6 = suspicious; 4 = fetus in jeopardy.**

## Non-stress test (NST)
Non-invasive: the fetal heart rate is traced with a cardiotocograph in relation to fetal movement. No contractions are induced.
- **Reactive (normal):** two or more accelerations of 15 bpm for 15 seconds in 20 minutes.
- **Non-reactive:** no accelerations with movement.

Safety: do not let the woman lie flat (supine hypotension); use a semi-sitting or left-side position.

## Next step
A non-reactive NST leads to a contraction stress test ([[Contraction Stress Test and Late Deceleration Response]]) or a BPP.

## How the exam asks about it
Reactive versus non-reactive, the normal score, and why not supine.

## Related topics
[[Contraction Stress Test and Late Deceleration Response]], [[Fetal Heart Rate Patterns and Decelerations]], [[Ultrasound in Pregnancy]]

title: Contraction Stress Test and Late Deceleration Response
body:
## What it is
Checks how the fetal heart responds to **uterine contractions**, to predict whether the placenta can cope with labor. Done when the NST is non-reactive ([[Biophysical Profile and Non-Stress Test]]); the handout places it at about 38 weeks.

## Results
- **Negative (normal):** no late decelerations with contractions.
- **Positive (abnormal):** late decelerations.

## How contractions are made
1. **Nipple stimulation:** warm packs first, rub the nipples in cycles, rest 2-4 minutes if no contractions, up to 4 cycles.
2. **Oxytocin challenge:** if nipple stimulation fails, give diluted oxytocin at a slowly increasing rate until two consecutive contractions occur, then stop the infusion and compare the contractions with the heart tracing.

Safety: observe about 30 minutes afterwards to be sure contractions settle and preterm labor does not start.

## If late decelerations appear (priority order)
1. Stop oxytocin (no more contractions wanted).
2. Turn the woman to her **left side** (relieves vena cava pressure, improves placental flow).
3. Give oxygen as ordered (the handout says 8-10 L/min).
4. Hydrate with IV fluids.
5. If decelerations persist, prepare for urgent delivery (cesarean).

## How the exam asks about it
"Positive CST" = bad; first action for late decelerations. See [[Fetal Heart Rate Patterns and Decelerations]] for pattern recognition.

## Check against your textbook
Handout drop rates for oxytocin and "plain water" hydration (it means IV fluid) should be checked against your local protocol.

## Related topics
[[Biophysical Profile and Non-Stress Test]], [[Fetal Heart Rate Patterns and Decelerations]]

title: Chorionic Villi Sampling and Alpha-Fetoprotein
body:
## Chorionic villi sampling (CVS)
A sample of chorionic villi from the developing placenta is taken for chromosome or DNA analysis. Done early, at **8-10 weeks** in the handout. After the procedure, tell her to **report chills or fever** (possible infection or threatened miscarriage).

## Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)
A protein made by the fetal liver; maternal serum levels peak between about 13 and 32 weeks.
- **Elevated** AFP: neural tube defects (also seen with multiple pregnancy, [[Multiple Pregnancy and Twin Types]]).
- **Decreased** AFP: chromosomal disorders such as Down syndrome.

## Why it matters
Both are screening/diagnostic steps for genetic problems. They help the family make informed decisions; the nurse supports and explains but does not decide for them. Also relevant to newborn follow-up ([[Newborn Screening]]).

## How the exam asks about it
Match the test to the finding (high AFP = neural tube defect) and to the gestational age.

## Check against your textbook
CVS is commonly placed at 10-13 weeks in many sources; AFP screening is usually 15-20 weeks. Confirm in your references.

## Related topics
[[Amniocentesis and Amniotic Fluid]], [[Ultrasound in Pregnancy]]

title: Maternal Psychological Tasks by Trimester
body:
## Core idea
The mother's attention moves from herself to the baby across the pregnancy.

- **First trimester:** accepting that she is pregnant, often with ambivalence. Concern for herself is greater than concern for the baby.
- **Second trimester:** accepting the baby as a real person (quickening helps). Concern for self and baby is about equal.
- **Third trimester:** accepting parenthood and preparing for birth. Concern for the baby exceeds concern for self.

## Nursing use
Match teaching to the stage: first trimester, symptom relief and reassurance; second, bonding (listening to heart tones, showing ultrasound); third, birth preparation and parenting classes. Accept ambivalence without judgment (therapeutic communication).

## How the exam asks about it
A statement from a woman at a certain visit ("I feel sick and tired, I am not sure I want this") is matched to the trimester task.

## Related topics
[[Signs of Pregnancy: Presumptive, Probable and Positive]], [[Puerperium: Involution and Rubin's Phases]]

title: Theories of Labor Onset and Preliminary Signs of Labor
body:
## Theories of why labor starts
- **Fetal signal:** the fetus is mature enough to live outside.
- **Oxytocin:** uterine oxytocin receptors increase near term.
- **Progesterone withdrawal:** progesterone stays high in preterm pregnancy and falls near term, allowing contractions.
- **Prostaglandin:** prostaglandins stimulate uterine contractions.

## Preliminary (early warning) signs
- **Lightening:** the fetus settles into the pelvis, easing breathing but adding bladder pressure. Primigravida: about 2 weeks before labor; multigravida: at the start of labor.
- **Strong Braxton-Hicks contractions** in the last days.
- **Burst of energy** (nesting), linked to epinephrine rise as progesterone drops.
- **Slight weight loss** of about 1-3 lb as fluid is excreted.
- **Cervical ripening:** soft ("butter-soft") cervix on pelvic exam.

## Nursing point
These signs mean labor is near, not that it has begun; the surest sign is progressive, productive contractions ([[True Labor versus False Labor]]).

## How the exam asks about it
Primigravida vs multigravida lightening timing, and which signs are "preliminary".

## Related topics
[[True Labor versus False Labor]], [[First Stage of Labor and Nitrazine Test]], [[Maternal Psychological Tasks by Trimester]]

title: Pelvis Types, Cephalopelvic Disproportion and Fetal Diameters
body:
## Pelvic types
- **Gynecoid:** the "normal" female pelvis, round inlet; best for birth.
- **Android:** male-type; narrow, acute pubic arch, narrow lower pelvis.
- **Anthropoid:** narrow transverse diameter, long anteroposterior diameter.
- **Platypelloid:** flat; oval inlet, shallow anteroposterior diameter.

## Cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD)
The fetal head is too large for the maternal pelvis. Even with CPD the usual plan is a **trial of labor**, not an automatic cesarean. The handout notes a hospital cesarean rate should stay under about 20%.

## Fetal head diameters
- **Suboccipitobregmatic:** smallest, about 9.5 cm (fully flexed head).
- **Occipitofrontal:** about 11 cm.
- **Occipitomental:** widest, about 13.5 cm (face/extended head).
A well-flexed head presents the smallest diameter, which is why flexion helps labor ([[Second Stage of Labor and Mechanisms of Labor]]).

## Fontanelles
- **Anterior:** diamond-shaped, closes at 12-18 months.
- **Posterior:** triangular, closes at 2-3 months.

## How the exam asks about it
Which pelvis is ideal, why CPD is not an absolute cesarean indication, and diamond vs triangle fontanelle.

## Check against your textbook
Posterior fontanelle closure is often given as 6-8 weeks; check.

## Related topics
[[Fetal Lie, Attitude, Presentation, Position and Station]], [[Second Stage of Labor and Mechanisms of Labor]]

title: Fetal Lie, Attitude, Presentation, Position and Station
body:
## Definitions
- **Lie:** relation of the baby's long axis to the mother's: longitudinal, transverse or oblique. A **transverse lie** means labor will not progress.
- **Attitude:** degree of flexion. Full flexion (vertex/occiput) presents the smallest diameter. Sinciput (military) is less flexed; brow is partly extended; **face** is the widest diameter and generally cannot enter the pelvis. Complete extension stops progress.
- **Presentation:** the body part that first meets the cervix (cephalic, breech, shoulder). Set by lie plus attitude.
- **Position:** presenting part relative to a quadrant of the mother's pelvis, e.g. ROP, LSA.

## Station
Level of the presenting part compared with the **ischial spines**.
- Above the spines: negative numbers, -3 floating up to -1.
- At the spines: **0 = engaged**.
- Below the spines: positive numbers up to +3 (crowning).

The linea terminalis divides the false pelvis (above) from the true pelvis (below).

## How the exam asks about it
Which station means engagement (0), which attitude is hopeless for vaginal entry (face), and which lie blocks dilation (transverse).

## Check against your textbook
The handout shows both sides of the spines with minus signs; standard teaching uses minus above and plus below.

## Related topics
[[Prenatal Visits, Blood Pressure and Leopold's Maneuvers]], [[Pelvis Types, Cephalopelvic Disproportion and Fetal Diameters]], [[Breech Presentation Types]]

title: True Labor versus False Labor
body:
## True labor
- Starts in the lower back, wraps to the front.
- Regular intervals that shorten.
- Increasing intensity.
- **Progressive cervical dilation and effacement.**
- Walking makes it stronger; sedation does not stop it.

## False labor
- Confined to the lower abdomen.
- Irregular, no change in intensity.
- **No cervical change.**
- Walking or sedation relieves it.

## Other signs labor has begun
- **Productive contractions** are the surest sign.
- **Bloody show:** expulsion of the mucus plug (operculum) as the cervix softens.
- **Rupture of membranes:** gush or slow leak of clear fluid.
- Cervical dilation.

## Nursing action
If unsure, assess contraction pattern and check cervical change; reassure a woman in false labor and advise when to return. Check fetal heart tones and note fluid color if membranes ruptured ([[First Stage of Labor and Nitrazine Test]]).

## How the exam asks about it
Tell true from false labor, and the sign that proves labor is real (cervical change).

## Related topics
[[Theories of Labor Onset and Preliminary Signs of Labor]], [[First Stage of Labor and Nitrazine Test]]

title: First Stage of Labor and Nitrazine Test
body:
## Definition
First stage = true contractions until the cervix is fully dilated (10 cm).

## Phases (LAT)
- **Latent:** 0-3 cm; mild contractions 20-40 seconds every 5-10 minutes; effacement; handout times: nullipara about 6 hours, multipara about 4.5 hours.
- **Active:** 4-7 cm; moderate contractions 40-60 seconds every 3-5 minutes.
- **Transition:** 8-10 cm; strongest contractions 60-90 seconds every 2-3 minutes. The most intense phase; coach breathing and give constant support.

## Nitrazine test
Checks whether leaking fluid is amniotic fluid. Nitrazine paper touched to vaginal fluid: **blue = alkaline = amniotic fluid**; **yellow/red-orange = acidic = urine** (the handout says red).

## Rupture of membranes
Check the fetal heart rate right after rupture (cord prolapse risk, [[Preterm Rupture of Membranes and Cord Prolapse]]). If membranes have been ruptured more than about 24 hours without birth, infection is likely and prompt delivery is planned.

## Priority nursing actions
Monitor contractions, fetal heart rate and maternal vital signs, offer position changes and comfort, keep her bladder empty. Do not encourage pushing before full dilation.

## How the exam asks about it
Match dilation to phase, and interpret nitrazine color.

## Related topics
[[True Labor versus False Labor]], [[Second Stage of Labor and Mechanisms of Labor]], [[Fetal Heart Rate Patterns and Decelerations]]

title: Second Stage of Labor and Mechanisms of Labor
body:
## Second stage
Full dilation (10 cm) until the baby is born. Handout durations: primigravida 1-4 hours, multigravida 20-45 minutes.

Key rules:
- Do not push before full dilation or without a contraction (it tires her and can swell the cervix).
- Pushing's main purpose is to shorten this stage.
- If she feels an urge to push before the cervix is ready, teach **pant-breathing**.

## Mechanisms of labor (cardinal movements)
The handout mnemonic ED FIRE ERE: **E**ngagement, **D**escent, **F**lexion, **I**nternal rotation, **E**xtension, **R**estitution/**E**xternal rotation, **E**xpulsion.

## Essential Intrapartum and Newborn Care (EINC)
- Properly timed cord clamping (when pulsations stop or after about 2 minutes, per the handout).
- Immediate drying (prevents hypothermia).
- No separation of mother and baby (skin-to-skin).
- Early breastfeeding within about 60 minutes. More in [[EINC and Active Management of Third Stage of Labor]].

## How the exam asks about it
Put the cardinal movements in order and name the EINC steps.

## Check against your textbook
Handout says cord clamping after pulsation stops or 2 minutes; current Philippine EINC wording is "1 to 3 minutes". Confirm.

## Related topics
[[First Stage of Labor and Nitrazine Test]], [[Third Stage of Labor: Placental Expulsion and Uterotonic Drugs]], [[Fetal Lie, Attitude, Presentation, Position and Station]]

title: Third Stage of Labor: Placental Expulsion and Uterotonic Drugs
body:
## Definition
Delivery of the baby until delivery of the placenta. Usually 5-10 minutes; beyond 30 minutes is abnormal. **Priority: prevent hemorrhage.**

## Signs of placental separation
- Uterus firm and globular (Calkin's sign) and rising.
- Cord lengthens.
- Sudden gush of blood.

## Schultze versus Duncan
- **Schultze:** fetal (shiny) side comes out first, separation from the center; less bleeding.
- **Duncan:** maternal (raw, red, rough) side first, separation from the edges; more bleeding.

## Inspecting the placenta
Check completeness (about 16-20 cotyledons), the membranes, and the cord: **two arteries and one vein (AVA)**. Retained fragments cause bleeding.

## Drugs
- **Oxytocin:** given diluted and slowly before delivery; larger amounts after the placenta is out, to keep the uterus contracted.
- **Ergot preparations (methylergonovine):** give **only after** the placenta is delivered; strong contraction beforehand can trap the placenta.

## How the exam asks about it
Timing of ergot drugs, Schultze vs Duncan, and how many vessels in the cord. Active management is in [[EINC and Active Management of Third Stage of Labor]].

## Check against your textbook
Handout infusion rates (11-12 drops/min) are not reliable; use your agency's protocol. Ergot drugs are avoided in hypertension.

## Related topics
[[Second Stage of Labor and Mechanisms of Labor]], [[Fourth Stage of Labor and Postpartum Checks]], [[Postpartum Hemorrhage]]
outlineRefs: Drugs for Third Stage of Labor

title: Fourth Stage of Labor and Postpartum Checks
body:
## Definition
The first 1-4 hours after the placenta comes out. Priority: **stabilize and prevent bleeding.**

## Why it is risky
Fluid shifts back into circulation, raising cardiac output and oxygen use. This stage is the hardest for women with heart disease ([[Heart Disease in Pregnancy]]).

## BUBBLE-HE assessment
- **B**reasts
- **U**terus (firm, midline, at or just below the navel)
- **B**ladder (full bladder pushes the uterus up and causes bleeding)
- **B**owels
- **L**ochia ([[Lochia and Return of Menstruation]])
- **E**pisiotomy/perineum
- **H**omans' sign (calf pain on dorsiflexion: possible thrombophlebitis, [[Postpartum Thrombophlebitis]])
- **E**motional status

## Priority nursing actions
Check vital signs, fundus and bleeding often. A boggy uterus: **massage the fundus first**, then help her empty the bladder. Keep the baby with her for bonding and breastfeeding.

## Check against your textbook
The handout lists the "E"s as Episiotomy and Homan's sign only; many texts add Emotional status.

## Related topics
[[Third Stage of Labor: Placental Expulsion and Uterotonic Drugs]], [[Postpartum Hemorrhage]], [[Puerperium: Involution and Rubin's Phases]]

title: Spontaneous and Induced Abortion
body:
## What it is
Loss of a pregnancy before the fetus is viable (the handout: over 24 weeks or at least 500 g counts as viable). Most spontaneous abortions are caused by **chromosomal defects** in the embryo.

## Types of spontaneous abortion
- **Threatened:** vaginal bleeding, **cervix closed** (no dilation or effacement). Pregnancy may continue.
- **Inevitable/imminent:** bleeding **with cervical dilation and effacement**; it cannot be stopped.
- **Incomplete:** some products of conception passed, some retained (bleeding continues).
- **Complete:** all products passed.
- **Habitual (recurrent):** three or more consecutive losses; a common cause is premature cervical dilation ([[Premature Cervical Dilation and Cerclage]]).

## Induced abortion
Deliberately ended pregnancy before viability: therapeutic (medical reasons) or illegal. Philippine law restricts abortion; the nurse gives non-judgmental care and supports the client.

## Priority nursing actions
Assess bleeding (pad count, tissue passed; save any tissue), vital signs, pain; watch for shock (airway, breathing, circulation first); provide emotional support for grief. Check Rh status for Rh-negative mothers (Rh immune globulin).

## How the exam asks about it
Distinguish threatened (closed cervix) from inevitable (open cervix), and incomplete from complete.

## Check against your textbook
Rh immune globulin and the legal wording are not in the handout; add from your references.

## Related topics
[[Ectopic Pregnancy]], [[Hydatidiform Mole]], [[Premature Cervical Dilation and Cerclage]]

title: Ectopic Pregnancy
body:
## What it is
Implantation outside the uterine cavity. Most often in the **ampulla** of the fallopian tube ([[Ovaries and Fallopian Tubes]]); interstitial is the most dangerous. Most common predisposing factor: **pelvic inflammatory disease**, plus previous tubal surgery, IUD use and previous ectopic pregnancy.

## Findings
- Classic triad: amenorrhea, vaginal spotting/bleeding, **unilateral lower abdominal pain**.
- Sharp, knife-like pain; pain on movement of the cervix.
- With rupture: rigid abdomen, falling blood pressure, shock signs, shoulder pain; bleeding inside the abdomen (hemoperitoneum), bluish navel (Cullen's sign).

## Diagnosis
Ultrasound, hCG levels, and **culdocentesis** (fluid from the rectouterine pouch via the vagina).

## Treatment
- **Methotrexate** IM for an unruptured ectopic under about 3 cm: stops fast-growing cells so the tissue is absorbed.
- **Salpingotomy** for an unruptured one, preserving the tube.
- **Salpingectomy** if ruptured.

## Priority nursing actions
A ruptured ectopic is a **life-threatening bleed**: ABCs, large IV access, treat shock ([[Management of Shock]]), prepare for surgery, keep NPO. Support grief afterwards.

## Check against your textbook
Rh immune globulin for Rh-negative clients and exact methotrexate criteria are not in the handout.

## Related topics
[[Spontaneous and Induced Abortion]], [[Ovaries and Fallopian Tubes]]

title: Hydatidiform Mole
body:
## What it is
Abnormal growth of the trophoblast: grape-like fluid-filled vesicles instead of a normal placenta (molar pregnancy / gestational trophoblastic disease). Cause unknown; risk factors in the handout: low protein intake, low socio-economic status, age under 18 or over 35.

## Findings
- Severe vomiting (very high hCG).
- Pinkish/brownish vaginal discharge or bleeding.
- **No fetal heart tones**; uterus larger than expected (rapid enlargement).
- Early hypertension in pregnancy.
- Ultrasound: "snowstorm" appearance ([[Ultrasound in Pregnancy]]).

## Management
- **Dilatation and curettage (suction)** to remove the tissue.
- **Monitor beta-hCG** every 2 weeks until normal, then every 2-4 weeks for a year (cancer risk: choriocarcinoma; spread to lungs and brain). The handout lists normal hCG as 100,000-400,000 and mole as 1-2 million units.
- **No pregnancy for one year**, so a rise in hCG can be recognized as recurrence.

## Priority nursing actions
Assess bleeding and shock, prepare for curettage, support grief, teach reliable contraception ([[Reproductive Health and Family Planning]]) and the need for follow-up.

## Check against your textbook
Handout hCG values may be mis-quoted and units unclear; verify.

## Related topics
[[Spontaneous and Induced Abortion]], [[Pregnancy-Induced Hypertension: Classification and Pre-eclampsia]]

title: Premature Cervical Dilation and Cerclage
body:
## What it is
Formerly "incompetent cervix": the cervix opens painlessly too early and cannot hold the pregnancy to term. The most common cause of **habitual abortion** ([[Spontaneous and Induced Abortion]]). First sign: pink-stained discharge or pelvic pressure.

## Causes
Defective cervical collagen, repeated cervical trauma, repeated dilatation and curettage.

## Treatment (cerclage)
- **McDonald:** purse-string suture around the cervix, placed before about 12-14 weeks (handout: under 12 weeks). Removed at about 37-38 weeks, then vaginal birth is possible.
- **Shirodkar:** tape placed under the cervical lining; typically left in place and the baby delivered by cesarean.

## Nursing responsibilities
Bed rest, **modified Trendelenburg** (hips higher than head to take pressure off the cervix), no intercourse, and tocolytics (terbutaline, ritodrine) if contractions start ([[Premature Labor and Tocolysis]]).

## How the exam asks about it
Which procedure is removed at term (McDonald) and the typical presentation (painless dilation).

## Check against your textbook
Handout says Shirodkar is placed transabdominally; the usual description is transvaginal (abdominal cerclage is a separate technique). Also, ritodrine is rarely used now.

## Related topics
[[Spontaneous and Induced Abortion]], [[Premature Labor and Tocolysis]]

title: Placenta Previa
body:
## What it is
The placenta implants low and covers or nears the cervical opening. Leading cause of **painless bright red bleeding** in the third trimester.

## Risk factors
Multiparity, previous cesarean scar or uterine surgery, uterine tumors, uterine anomalies (e.g. bicornuate).

## Types
Low-lying, marginal (reaches the edge of the os), partial (covers part), total (covers all).

## Findings
Sudden, painless, bright red bleeding; **soft, non-tender uterus**.

## Priority nursing actions (safety of mother and fetus)
- **Never do a vaginal, pelvic or rectal exam** (could trigger massive hemorrhage). Ultrasound confirms.
- Bed rest, side-lying position.
- Baseline vital signs, then check often (every 5-15 minutes when bleeding).
- IV access; hourly urine output.
- External monitoring of fetal heart rate and contractions; oxygen available.
- Ask about timing, amount (cups/tablespoons) and color of bleeding.
- If bleeding stops, bed rest at home with follow-up; a total previa needs cesarean.

## How the exam asks about it
Compare with [[Abruptio Placentae]]: previa = painless, soft uterus; abruptio = painful, rigid uterus.

## Related topics
[[Abruptio Placentae]], [[Ultrasound in Pregnancy]], [[Multiple Pregnancy and Twin Types]]

title: Abruptio Placentae
body:
## What it is
Premature separation of a normally placed placenta before the baby is born. Cause unknown.

## Risk factors
Cocaine use, smoking, high parity, older age, short cord, chronic hypertension and pregnancy-induced hypertension ([[Pregnancy-Induced Hypertension: Classification and Pre-eclampsia]]).

## Findings
- **Sharp, stabbing uterine pain**, board-like **rigid** uterus.
- Bleeding may be heavy, scant or hidden (concealed).
- Fetal heart tones weak or absent.
- Signs of shock out of proportion to visible blood.

## Types
- **Peripheral:** blood escapes through the vagina; safer.
- **Central (concealed):** blood stays in the uterus; more dangerous. **Couvelaire uterus** (bluish/copper uterus, bleeding into the muscle), atony, and often hysterectomy.

## Priority nursing actions
Treat as an emergency: fluids and blood, oxygen, external fetal monitoring, vital signs every 5-15 minutes, **lateral position**, **no abdominal, vaginal or pelvic exams**, urgent delivery if fetal distress.

## How the exam asks about it
Painful bleeding with a rigid uterus = abruptio; compare with [[Placenta Previa]]. Also linked to DIC.

## Check against your textbook
Handout says separation occurs in the second stage; it can occur any time after 20 weeks. Verify.

## Related topics
[[Placenta Previa]], [[Postpartum Hemorrhage]], [[Pregnancy-Induced Hypertension: Classification and Pre-eclampsia]]

title: Preterm Rupture of Membranes and Cord Prolapse
body:
## What it is
Membranes rupture before labor and before 37 weeks (preterm PROM). Causes: unknown, or infection of the membranes (chorioamnionitis).

## Complications
- **Infection:** risk rises sharply after about 24 hours of rupture; leads to sepsis.
- **Cord prolapse:** cord slips below the presenting part and is compressed: an emergency.

## Management
- Bed rest, monitor temperature and fetal heart.
- Corticosteroids (betamethasone) to speed fetal lung maturity.
- Delivery if infection, fetal distress or labor.

## Cord prolapse: priority actions
1. Call for help; **do not push the cord back**.
2. Relieve pressure: gloved hand lifts the presenting part off the cord, knee-chest or Trendelenburg position.
3. Cover the cord with moist sterile saline gauze.
4. Give oxygen, monitor fetal heart, prepare for urgent cesarean.
Why: airway and circulation of the fetus come first.

## How the exam asks about it
First action for a visible cord and which position helps. Linked to [[Breech Presentation Types]] and [[Fetal Heart Rate Patterns and Decelerations]].

## Related topics
[[Premature Labor and Tocolysis]], [[Breech Presentation Types]], [[First Stage of Labor and Nitrazine Test]]

title: Premature Labor and Tocolysis
body:
## What it is
Labor before the end of 37 weeks; accounts for most neonatal deaths and is largely preventable.

## Causes and risks
Dehydration, urinary tract infection, periodontal disease, chorioamnionitis; adolescents, inadequate prenatal care, stressful work.

## Management
- Bed rest (less pressure on the cervix).
- IV hydration (may halt contractions).
- **Tocolytics** to slow labor (e.g. terbutaline, magnesium sulfate); corticosteroids to mature the fetal lungs ([[Preterm Rupture of Membranes and Cord Prolapse]]).
- No intercourse.

## Priority nursing actions
Assess contractions, fluid loss and fetal heart; position on the left side; teach warning signs (regular contractions, back pain, pelvic pressure, fluid leak). Watch tocolytic effects (terbutaline raises maternal and fetal heart rate; magnesium: see [[Magnesium Sulfate and Eclampsia Care]]).

## How the exam asks about it
Which interventions delay preterm labor and what teaching to give.

## Related topics
[[Premature Cervical Dilation and Cerclage]], [[Preterm Rupture of Membranes and Cord Prolapse]]

title: Post-term Pregnancy
body:
## What it is
Pregnancy lasting beyond **42 weeks** (also post-dates). Occurs in about 3-12% of pregnancies.

## Possible causes
Heavy salicylate use (blocks prostaglandin needed to start labor, [[Drugs to Avoid in Pregnancy: NSAIDs and Aspirin]]) and a uterus that does not respond to normal labor triggers.

## Risks
Meconium aspiration, macrosomia (big baby), decreased placental function.

## Management
Cervical ripening with prostaglandin gel or misoprostol, oxytocin to induce, close fetal heart monitoring; non-stress test and biophysical profile ([[Biophysical Profile and Non-Stress Test]]).

## How the exam asks about it
Define post-term and name the main fetal complications.

## Related topics
[[Precipitate Labor]], [[Biophysical Profile and Non-Stress Test]]

title: Precipitate Labor
body:
## What it is
Labor so rapid it lasts under 3 hours. Precipitate dilation is 5 cm or more per hour in first-time mothers, or 10 cm or more per hour in women who have given birth before.

## Dangers
- Unplanned birth outside hospital: infection risk to the baby.
- Maternal laceration and hemorrhage.
- Fetal head trauma and intracranial bleeding.

## Priority nursing actions
Stay with the woman, do not leave her alone, prepare for birth where she is, call for help, support the head and control delivery, keep the baby warm, and watch for postpartum hemorrhage ([[Postpartum Hemorrhage]]). Do not try to delay birth.

## How the exam asks about it
Define precipitate labor and the first action (stay with her).

## Related topics
[[Post-term Pregnancy]], [[Postpartum Hemorrhage]]

title: Breech Presentation Types
body:
## What it is
Buttocks or feet present first at the cervix; about 3% of births.

## Types
- **Complete:** thighs and legs flexed, baby "sitting"; buttocks and feet both present.
- **Frank:** hips flexed, knees extended; buttocks alone present.
- **Footling:** one (single) or both (double) feet present; neither thigh nor knee flexed.

## Problems
Cord prolapse ([[Preterm Rupture of Membranes and Cord Prolapse]]), head entrapment, shoulder problems. **Meconium staining is expected** in breech (squeezing of the bowel) and is not itself a sign of distress.

## Nursing points
Leopold's first maneuver finds a soft, less defined mass in the fundus ([[Prenatal Visits, Blood Pressure and Leopold's Maneuvers]]). Fetal heart is best heard higher on the abdomen. Prepare for possible cesarean and watch for cord prolapse after membranes rupture.

## How the exam asks about it
Identify the breech type, and the meconium fact.

## Related topics
[[Fetal Lie, Attitude, Presentation, Position and Station]], [[Prenatal Visits, Blood Pressure and Leopold's Maneuvers]]

title: Multiple Pregnancy and Twin Types
body:
## What it is
More than one fetus; 2-3% of births.

## Twin types
- **Monozygotic (identical):** one ovum and one sperm that splits; always the same sex. The handout says one placenta, one chorion and two amnions.
- **Dizygotic (fraternal):** two ova and two sperm; two placentas, chorions and amnions; same or different sex.

## Findings
Uterus larger than dates, high AFP ([[Chorionic Villi Sampling and Alpha-Fetoprotein]]), movement felt in several places, multiple sacs on ultrasound.

## Complications
Hypertension of pregnancy, hydramnios, placenta previa ([[Placenta Previa]]), preterm labor, anemia, postpartum hemorrhage, low birth weight, congenital anomalies.

## Nursing points
Closer prenatal follow-up, nutrition and iron, rest, early recognition of preterm labor ([[Premature Labor and Tocolysis]]).

## Check against your textbook
Monozygotic twins can have different membrane arrangements depending on when the split occurs.

## Related topics
[[Fundic Height Landmarks in Pregnancy]], [[Pregnancy-Induced Hypertension: Classification and Pre-eclampsia]]

title: Pregnancy-Induced Hypertension: Classification and Pre-eclampsia
body:
## What it is
Vasospasm in pregnancy affecting small and large arteries. Cause unknown. Classic signs: **hypertension after 20 weeks, proteinuria, edema** (plus vision changes in severe forms).

## Classification
- **Gestational hypertension:** BP 140/90 or higher, no proteinuria or edema; returns to normal after birth.
- **Mild pre-eclampsia:** BP 140/90 (or systolic up 30 / diastolic up 15 over baseline), proteinuria 1+ to 2+, weight gain over 2 lb a week (2nd trimester). The **diastolic** reading best reflects arterial spasm.
- **Severe pre-eclampsia:** BP about 160/110, proteinuria 3+ to 4+ (over 5 g/24 h), extensive edema, creatinine over 1.2 mg/dL, epigastric pain, liver problems, low platelets.
- **Eclampsia:** seizures or coma on top of pre-eclampsia ([[Magnesium Sulfate and Eclampsia Care]]).

## Management of mild disease
Rest (conserves oxygen, reduces vasospasm), **normal salt intake (not restricted)**, weekly checks. The handout says salt restriction can activate the renin-angiotensin system.

## Priority nursing actions
Monitor BP, reflexes, urine, edema, headache and visual changes; prevent seizures. Severe: magnesium sulfate, quiet environment.

## How the exam asks about it
Match findings to severity; recognize epigastric pain and headache as severe warning signs.

## Related topics
[[Magnesium Sulfate and Eclampsia Care]], [[HELLP Syndrome]], [[Abruptio Placentae]]

title: Magnesium Sulfate and Eclampsia Care
body:
## Magnesium sulfate
The drug to **prevent and treat seizures** in severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia.

Before each dose, check (toxicity signs):
- **Deep tendon reflexes** (absent = toxicity).
- **Respiratory rate** (under about 12/min = respiratory depression).
- **Urine output** (at least about 30 mL/hour; magnesium is cleared by the kidneys).
- Blood pressure (may drop).

**Antidote: calcium gluconate** at the bedside.

## Eclampsia
Most severe PIH: generalized seizure or coma plus pre-eclampsia signs. The handout lists additional drugs such as furosemide, hydralazine (for hypertension) and sedatives.

## Seizure precautions and care
- Dim, quiet room; limit visitors.
- Side rails up; suction at bedside.
- During a seizure: **nothing in the mouth**, turn to side to drain saliva, loosen clothing, protect from injury, note duration. After: airway, oxygen, then check fetal heart.
- Airway comes first, then safety, then medication (ABCs).

## Check against your textbook
Handout items such as digoxin with potassium and barbiturates for eclampsia are not standard; verify. Monitor magnesium blood level per protocol.

## Related topics
[[Pregnancy-Induced Hypertension: Classification and Pre-eclampsia]], [[HELLP Syndrome]], [[Premature Labor and Tocolysis]]

title: HELLP Syndrome
body:
## What it is
A severe complication of pre-eclampsia: **H**emolysis, **E**levated **L**iver enzymes, **L**ow **P**latelets. Occurs in about 4-12% of PIH cases; high maternal and infant mortality in the handout.

## Findings
Epigastric or right-upper-quadrant pain (liver), nausea, malaise, high BP, proteinuria, edema.

## Management
- Transfuse fresh-frozen plasma or platelets as ordered.
- Treat low blood sugar with IV glucose.
- Epidural may be avoided because of low platelets and bleeding risk.
- Prepare for early delivery; give magnesium for seizure prevention ([[Magnesium Sulfate and Eclampsia Care]]).

## Priority nursing actions
Monitor BP, bleeding, labs, urine output; report RUQ pain immediately.

## Check against your textbook
The handout heading "Laboratory studies" lists treatments instead of labs; labs are hemolysis markers, liver enzymes and platelet count.

## Related topics
[[Pregnancy-Induced Hypertension: Classification and Pre-eclampsia]], [[Magnesium Sulfate and Eclampsia Care]]

title: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus
body:
## What it is
Abnormal glucose handling that first appears in pregnancy; placental hormones such as human placental lactogen make the body resist insulin.

## Risk factors
Obesity, age over 25, family history, previous large baby (10 lb or more), unexplained fetal loss, previous anomalies.

## Screening and diagnosis
- **50-g oral glucose** at 24-28 weeks; blood drawn after 1 hour. Over 140 mg/dL leads to a 100-g 3-hour test.
- Diagnosis if two of four values are abnormal or the fasting value is above 95 mg/dL.

## Management
- Diet about 1,800-2,400 kcal/day; complex carbohydrates, avoid simple sugars and saturated fat.
- Exercise suitable for gestational age.
- **Insulin** when diet fails. The handout says oral hypoglycemics are teratogenic.

## Priority nursing actions
Teach home glucose checks, signs of hypo/hyperglycemia, and follow-up testing after birth (diabetes risk later). Newborn: watch for low blood sugar ([[Maternal and Child Health]]).

## Check against your textbook
Some guidelines now allow certain oral agents; cutoffs differ between guidelines.

## Related topics
[[Pregnancy-Induced Hypertension: Classification and Pre-eclampsia]], [[Multiple Pregnancy and Twin Types]]

title: Heart Disease in Pregnancy
body:
## Functional classes
- **Class I:** uncompromised; ordinary activity causes no discomfort.
- **Class II:** slightly compromised; ordinary activity gives fatigue, palpitations, dyspnea or angina.
- **Class III:** markedly compromised; symptoms with less than ordinary activity.
- **Class IV:** severely compromised; symptoms at rest or any activity.

Classes I and II can usually go through pregnancy; III and IV are poor candidates (counseled against pregnancy).

## Why pregnancy is risky
Cardiac output rises 25-50% ([[Body Changes in Pregnancy: Heart, Blood and Lungs]]). The most dangerous time is just after delivery, when retained fluid returns to circulation ([[Fourth Stage of Labor and Postpartum Checks]]).

## Priority nursing actions
Rest, left side lying, limit exertion, monitor for heart failure signs (dyspnea, cough, edema, rapid pulse), avoid prolonged pushing, supportive anesthesia.

## How the exam asks about it
Which class allows pregnancy, and the highest-risk period (fourth stage).

## Related topics
[[Body Changes in Pregnancy: Heart, Blood and Lungs]], [[Fourth Stage of Labor and Postpartum Checks]]

title: Fetal Heart Rate Patterns and Decelerations
body:
## Variability
Fluctuation of the fetal heart rate is one of the most reliable signs of fetal well-being.

## Patterns
- **Acceleration:** temporary rise with movement, a position change or analgesic; reassuring.
- **Early deceleration:** starts and ends with the contraction; **head compression**; benign late in labor. Early in labor it may indicate cephalopelvic disproportion ([[Pelvis Types, Cephalopelvic Disproportion and Fetal Diameters]]).
- **Late deceleration:** begins 30-40 seconds after contraction onset and recovers late; **uteroplacental insufficiency**; ominous.
- **Variable deceleration:** unpredictable shape and timing; **cord compression**.

## Priority actions
- **Late:** slow/stop oxytocin, turn to left side, give IV fluid and oxygen, prepare for rapid delivery if persistent ([[Contraction Stress Test and Late Deceleration Response]]).
- **Variable:** change position (side-lying or knee-chest), consider **amnioinfusion** (fluid into the uterus to cushion the cord).

## Memory aid
"VEAL CHOP": Variable = Cord compression, Early = Head compression, Acceleration = OK, Late = Placental insufficiency (common textbook mnemonic).

## How the exam asks about it
Match pattern to cause, and the first nursing action.

## Related topics
[[Contraction Stress Test and Late Deceleration Response]], [[Biophysical Profile and Non-Stress Test]], [[Preterm Rupture of Membranes and Cord Prolapse]]

title: Puerperium: Involution and Rubin's Phases
body:
## Puerperium
The 6 weeks after birth. Main priority: **involution**, the return of reproductive organs to the non-pregnant state; the fundus normally drops about one fingerbreadth (1 cm) a day. Other tasks: lactation, return of menstrual cycle, and parenting role.

## Rubin's phases
- **Taking-in (first 1-2 days):** the mother is passive and dependent; wants to retell her labor; hungry and tired. Reluctance for rooming-in can be normal.
- **Taking-hold (about days 2-7):** she starts to act independently, prefers to make her own decisions and learn newborn care; the best time for teaching. The handout says postpartum psychosis may show during this period; blues and depression more broadly belong to later weeks.
- **Letting-go:** she accepts the real baby and her new role.

## Nursing actions
Match care to phase: take-in = meet needs and listen; take-hold = teach; let-go = support. Assess for postpartum depression and bonding.

## Check against your textbook
Phase timing is not in the handout; the days above come from common textbooks. Postpartum psychosis timing is looser than stated.

## Related topics
[[Lochia and Return of Menstruation]], [[Fourth Stage of Labor and Postpartum Checks]], [[Maternal Psychological Tasks by Trimester]]

title: Lochia and Return of Menstruation
body:
## Lochia stages
- **Rubra:** days 1-3; bright red.
- **Serosa:** days 3-10; pink to brown.
- **Alba:** day 10 to 3rd-6th week; white-yellowish. After six weeks lochia should be gone.

Lochia occurs after cesarean births too.

## Normal versus abnormal
- Normal smell: musty, fleshy; **foul smell = infection**.
- Color should not be cloudy-yellow early (infection).
- Stages never reverse; **return to red** suggests retained placental fragments or hemorrhage.

## Return of menstruation
- Not breastfeeding: about 6-10 weeks.
- Breastfeeding: often months (about 6) ; lactation amenorrhea method needs exclusive breastfeeding, no menses, and within 6 months postpartum.
- Intercourse is usually allowed after 3-4 weeks per the handout.
- Breastfeeding is not a guaranteed contraceptive; see [[Reproductive Health and Family Planning]].

## How the exam asks about it
Name the lochia stage by day and color; spot the abnormal sign.

## Related topics
[[Puerperium: Involution and Rubin's Phases]], [[Postpartum Infection and Endometritis]], [[Postpartum Hemorrhage]]

title: Postpartum Hemorrhage
body:
## What it is
Excess bleeding after birth.
- **Early:** within 24 hours. **Most common cause: uterine atony** (soft, boggy uterus); second: lacerations; also clotting disorders.
- **Late:** after 24 hours. Causes: retained placental fragments, then hematoma.

## Priority nursing actions
1. **Massage the fundus** until firm (stops atony).
2. Empty the bladder (a full bladder displaces the uterus).
3. Give uterotonics as ordered ([[Third Stage of Labor: Placental Expulsion and Uterotonic Drugs]]).
4. Call for help, IV access, oxygen, monitor vital signs and urine; treat shock ([[Management of Shock]]).
5. Inspect for lacerations or retained tissue.
Why: circulation (stop the bleeding) before everything else.

## How the exam asks about it
A boggy uterus with heavy bleeding: massage first. See [[Abruptio Placentae]] for atony from Couvelaire uterus.

## Related topics
[[Third Stage of Labor: Placental Expulsion and Uterotonic Drugs]], [[Fourth Stage of Labor and Postpartum Checks]], [[BEmOC and CEmOC]]

title: Postpartum Infection and Endometritis
body:
## Postpartum infection
Often caused by the woman's own bacteria moving up into the uterus (endogenous).

## Endometritis
Infection of the uterine lining.
- Fever above 38 C, foul-smelling lochia, uterine or abdominal tenderness.
- Treatment: **antibiotics**, **semi-Fowler's position** (helps drainage).
- If untreated it can progress to **thrombophlebitis** ([[Postpartum Thrombophlebitis]]).

## Perineal / episiotomy infection
Antibiotics; surgical care may include removing sutures and draining pus.

## Nursing actions
Perineal hygiene (front to back), hand hygiene, assess lochia, temperature and wound ([[Lochia and Return of Menstruation]]), teach signs to report.

## How the exam asks about it
Fever + foul lochia + tender uterus = endometritis, and the position of choice.

## Related topics
[[Lochia and Return of Menstruation]], [[Postpartum Thrombophlebitis]]

title: Postpartum Thrombophlebitis
body:
## What it is
Clot formation with vein inflammation, usually in the lower legs, in the puerperium. Endometritis is a risk precursor ([[Postpartum Infection and Endometritis]]).

## Assessment
- Calf pain, warmth, swelling.
- **Homans' sign:** with the leg extended, dorsiflex the foot; calf pain is a positive sign.

## Management
- Antibiotics where infection exists.
- Anticoagulant **heparin** (monitor aPTT; antidote protamine sulfate).
- Rest with leg elevated; **do not massage the leg** (an embolus could move to the lungs).

## Priority red flag
Sudden chest pain, dyspnea or anxiety suggests pulmonary embolism: airway/breathing first, call for help.

## Check against your textbook
Homans' sign is no longer considered reliable; confirm. Heparin lab details and "do not massage" are added from general knowledge.

## Related topics
[[Postpartum Infection and Endometritis]], [[Fourth Stage of Labor and Postpartum Checks]]
